qrdBas-ae1109-d1e101.summary: Rubric introducing the first question on the first prologue of Book 1 of the Sentences.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e108.summary: States the question: whether a pure wayfarer (viator) can possibly have some evident cognition (of God) other than what can be had through the natural sciences.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e121.summary: First argument for the negative: such cognition would be either a priori, which is impossible since nothing is prior to God, or a posteriori, but all a posteriori cognition of God can be had naturally.
claims: Nothing is prior to God, so there is no a priori cognition of him.
All a posteriori cognition of God is naturally attainable.
concepts: a priori and a posteriori demonstration

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e137.summary: Second argument for the negative: the cognition would be either intuitive, which beatifies and so removes one from the state of the wayfarer, or abstractive, but the divine essence by its nature does not abstract.
claims: Intuitive cognition of God beatifies and ends the wayfarer state.
The divine essence is not abstractable.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e149.summary: Third argument for the negative: such cognition would be a mean between faith and vision (above faith because evident from the object, below vision because not beatifying), and a mean is incompossible with both extremes, as pale with white and black; but no wayfarer's cognition is incompossible with faith. The last words begin the counter-argument continued in the next paragraph.
claims: Such cognition would be an intermediate between faith and vision.
An intermediate is incompossible with both extremes.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e167.summary: Argument for the affirmative: what implies no contradiction from its terms is absolutely possible; a wayfarer's having such cognition implies none (as will be shown more fully later).
claims: What implies no contradiction in its terms is absolutely possible.
A wayfarer's evident cognition of God implies no contradiction.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e183.summary: Announces the order of procedure for the question.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e188.summary: First step of the plan: clarify the terms of the question and some preliminaries.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e195.summary: Second step: set out others' opinions by articles, with their reasons.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e200.summary: Third step: give the author's own answer by arguing against the others' opinions.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e208.summary: Fourth step: resolve the others' reasons.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e213.summary: Fifth step: answer the principal arguments.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e218.summary: A fragmentary paragraph mark ('Pri-'), evidently the start of 'Primo', continued in the next paragraph.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e220.summary: Begins the first step by listing the terms to be clarified: first, what is meant by 'wayfarer'.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e227.summary: Second term to be clarified: what is meant by cognition evident from the object.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e232.summary: Third item: a distinction regarding such cognition.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e238.summary: Fourth item: power and the possible.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e243.summary: Defines the pure wayfarer: one who has not reached the end of beatitude but tends toward formal beatitude (by which one is perfected in God, objective beatitude) chiefly through faith and hope, as a traveler to Rome tends toward the city and ceases to be a traveler on arrival. The paragraph closes by beginning the second definition, continued next.
claims: A wayfarer is one tending toward but not yet possessing beatitude, chiefly through faith and hope.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e280.summary: Defines cognition evident from the object: that to which the intellect assents by the force of the object and its own natural power, without the will's command contributing to the assent. The will can turn the intellect toward or away from objects (at least after the first intellection), but cannot cause evident assent. Faith is therefore not evident, since however turned to its object the intellect assents only by the will's command (Augustine).
claims: Evident cognition is assent caused by the object and the intellect's natural power, not commanded by the will.
The will can direct the intellect's attention but not produce evident assent.
Faith is not evident, since its assent depends on the will's command.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e317.summary: Third preliminary: evident intellectual cognition is twofold, abstractive and intuitive. Intuitive cognition is defined as that which concerns its per se primary object as existing (in act or potency) in its own nature and really present outside to the knower.
claims: Evident cognition is either intuitive or abstractive.
Intuitive cognition concerns its per se primary object as existing and really present.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e330.summary: Explains the definition: cognition is characterized by its object, as powers are (De anima II), and by its per se object, since accidental objects are indeterminate and cannot define anything (as Aristotle sets aside accidental being in Metaphysics VI).
claims: Cognitions, like powers, are defined by their per se objects.
Accidental objects cannot ground a definition.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e354.summary: Explains 'primary object': a cognition is specified only by its primary object, so for intuition only the primary object need coexist. Hence God's eternal knowledge of non-existent creatures was truly intuitive, since creatures were secondary objects eminently contained in and represented by the divine essence, the primary object. This is argued from God's immutability and perfection, from the identity of God's knowledge of his essence and of creatures, and from Augustine (De trinitate XV; De civitate XI) that God knew things to be made just as he knew them made. God likewise knows negations and impossibles intuitively.
claims: Intuitive cognition requires only that its primary object exist and be present.
God's eternal knowledge of creatures, including non-existent ones, is intuitive.
God knows creatures as secondary objects in his essence as primary object.
God knows negations and impossibles intuitively.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e420.summary: Explains 'existing in act in its own nature', which holds naturally and by common law, unlike abstractive cognition, whose primary object need not exist, as a rose is understood abstractively when none exists or is present.
claims: By common law, intuitive cognition requires an existing object; abstractive cognition does not.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e442.summary: Explains the addition 'or in potency' to exclude the view that intuition absolutely requires its object to exist and be present. Since intuitive cognition is an absolute quality essentially distinct from its created object, which relates to it as an extrinsic secondary cause, God can conserve the cognition without the object (what God does with secondary causes he can do without them). So there can be vision without anything visible, as an accident without a subject. The objection that something seen that does not exist is unintelligible is answered: the vision exists, and what is denominated 'seen' (by extrinsic, intentional denomination) does not exist, as with knowledge.
claims: Intuitive cognition does not absolutely require the existence of its object.
God can produce intuitive cognition of a non-existent created object.
What God can do with secondary causes he can do without them.
'Seen' is an extrinsic, intentional denomination that need not correspond to an existing thing.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e499.summary: The sensible species is not required for vision as a representation of the object; species and vision are two ordered effects of the object, neither causing the other, so the eye could see naturally without species. Against the Commentator (De somno) on illusions and the fire-circle, the author replies that strong intentions are produced in the nearby medium, as the colour cast by sunlight through glass, or by demons in magical illusions; or that the Commentator is speaking of imagination. He then states the main criterion: abstractive cognition is always mediated by something representative, while intuitive cognition is immediate, with no medium as known object or as representation, only as ratio cognoscendi. Even a species actuating the power would not abolish intuition.
claims: Sensible species are not necessary representations for vision; species and vision are co-effects of the object.
Sensory illusions involve strong intentions in the medium, not vision of the non-existent.
Abstractive cognition is always mediated by a representative; intuitive cognition is immediate.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e601.summary: Even a visible species in sight would not abolish intuition, so what most distinguishes intuitive cognition is immediacy, while abstractive cognition is naturally always mediated (though God could produce it without a medium). Rejects an addition by others that intuition requires the object's presence 'in the ratio of object' and not just real presence by essence, presence, and power (so that God is seen in heaven but not on the way). Since God beatifies by his essence and real existence, being present 'as object' adds nothing real beyond essential and existential presence except a relation of reason. God is therefore as present, on the object's side, to wayfarers and the damned as to the blessed.
claims: Immediacy is the chief mark of intuitive cognition.
God could produce abstractive cognition without a representative medium.
Being present 'as object' adds nothing real to real presence.
On the side of the object, God is equally present to wayfarers, the damned, and the blessed.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e671.summary: Defines abstractive cognition as one lacking some condition of intuitive cognition: by common law it does not concern its primary object as existing and really present, nor as immediately known, but always through some actual medium (naturally) or aptitudinally (when caused by God alone). Hence all our natural intellectual cognition is abstractive, mediated by phantasms or intelligible species, and its possibility is undoubted.
claims: Abstractive cognition is cognition mediated by a representative.
All natural human intellectual cognition is abstractive.
Phantasms or intelligible species mediate our natural understanding.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e708.summary: The real doubt is whether intellectual intuitive cognition is possible for us, since we hardly experience it. Scotus's argument (Quodlibet q.6) is adduced: every perfection of sensitive cognition can belong eminently to intellectual cognition; sense attains its object as existing and present, not merely in a diminished likeness; so the intellect can too. Paul (1 Cor 13, 'face to face') and John ('we shall see him as he is') attest such cognition, identical with facial vision.
claims: Every perfection of sensitive cognition can belong eminently to intellectual cognition.
The intellect can attain its object as existing and present, so intellectual intuition is possible.
Scripture attests facial vision of God.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e759.summary: First corollary: anything that can exist outside the intellect really present to the knower, whether essence or existence, substance or accident (at least absolutes; relations are doubtful), can be the primary object of intellectual intuition. Anything that can be present in a representative can be the primary object of abstractive cognition.
claims: Any absolute capable of real presence can be a primary object of intuition.
It is doubtful whether relations can be primary objects of cognition.
Anything representable can be a primary object of abstractive cognition.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e785.summary: Second corollary: abstractive cognition is not so called because it abstracts from actual existence as the known content, since actual existence itself can be known abstractively through a representative. It is so called because it abstracts from the real existence and presence of the object in its own nature; that its object exists is accidental to it, since the representative represents the object indifferently whether or not it exists.
claims: Abstractive cognition can represent existence itself.
Its abstraction is from the real existence and presence of the object, not from existence as content.
The representative represents indifferently whether the object exists.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e814.summary: Third corollary: existence and presence, conditions of the intuitive object, can also be intrinsic conditions of some abstractive object, at least existence. So intuitive and abstractive cognition can be of the very same object under the same objective ratio ('I believe and will see the same thing under the same ratio'). But the third condition, immediacy, cannot belong to an abstractive object, nor mediacy to an intuitive one, so they are distinguished chiefly by mediate versus immediate.
claims: Intuitive and abstractive cognition can share the same object under the same objective ratio.
They are distinguished chiefly by immediacy versus mediacy.
concepts: same object of faith and vision

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e858.summary: On 'scientific' in the question's title: propter quid scientific cognition is twofold. Virtually, it is the simple cognition of subject, middle term, or principle, which causally contains knowledge of attributes and conclusions (as heat contains heat). Formally, it is the evident cognition of a conclusion deduced from necessary first truths and causes; this is science in the proper sense, always complex and mediate. Only propter quid knowledge matters here, since it is commonly agreed that evident (quia) knowledge of God from creatures is possible.
claims: Scientific cognition is either virtual (of subject or principle) or formal (of conclusions).
Formal science is always complex and of mediate truths.
Evident a posteriori knowledge of God from creatures is commonly granted.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e912.summary: Distinguishes natural from supernatural possibility. What is naturally possible is attainable from natural principles and causes under God's general concurrence (an ass generates, fire heats). What is supernaturally possible is not repugnant but attainable only by divine power with special influence, as infused charity. God does not infuse in common many perfections he could by absolute power, since he has not so ordained. The evident cognition in question, if possible, would be of this kind, given to very few by special grace. The paragraph ends by beginning to restate the question.
claims: Natural possibility is attainability from natural causes under general concurrence.
Supernatural possibility is attainability only by special divine influence.
God does not in common confer all he could by absolute power.
Evident cognition of God for a wayfarer, if possible, is supernaturally possible.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e962.summary: Restates the question in light of the preliminaries: whether by any power it is possible for a pure wayfarer to have evident scientific cognition of God beyond what can be naturally acquired from creatures.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e976.summary: Reports a first opinion: since intuition removes one from the wayfarer state, and abstractive cognition of the divine essence is simply impossible to a wayfarer by any power, neither simple cognition of the essence (virtual science) nor complex formal science of God is possible.
claims: No abstractive cognition of the divine essence is possible to a wayfarer by any power.
Therefore no theological science, virtual or formal, is possible for a wayfarer.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e994.summary: First argument for the opinion: what is impossible in the essentially prior is impossible in the posterior; intuitive cognition of God is essentially prior to abstractive, since all abstraction derives from intuition. God knows other things abstractively through intuition of his essence, angels by intuiting their own essence, and we only after sensing (nothing in the intellect not first in the sense). So since intuition of God is impossible to wayfarers, so is abstraction.
claims: Abstractive cognition always derives from prior intuitive cognition.
Since intuition of God is impossible to a wayfarer, so is abstractive cognition of God.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1029.summary: Second argument: what is known abstractively is known only as a being in potency and imperfect, since abstraction prescinds from actual existence; God is pure act and necessary being.
claims: Abstractive cognition represents its object as potential and imperfect.
God, as pure act, cannot be so represented.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1045.summary: Third argument: being in potency, the object of abstraction, is known only through being in act (Metaphysics IX); being in act known as present yields intuition; so abstractive cognition of God presupposes intuition.
claims: Potential being is known only through actual being.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1061.summary: Fourth argument: if abstractive cognition could exist without prior intuition, knowledge would not be really related to its object, since it could be of the non-existent, and there is no real relation to non-being, contrary to Aristotle (Metaphysics V).
claims: Knowledge bears a real relation to its object.
Abstraction without prior intuition would sever this relation.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1077.summary: Fifth argument: a wayfarer's abstractive cognition of God would be more, equally, or less perfect than intuitive cognition. It cannot be more or equally perfect, for then it would beatify. It cannot be less perfect, because God's eternal knowledge of creatures, which did not exist and so was abstractive, is most perfect.
claims: An abstractive cognition of God cannot be ranked consistently relative to intuition.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1096.summary: Sixth argument: what is known in itself, as object, and present is known intuitively; on the proponent's view God is known in himself and is present by the supposed abstractive cognition, so it would be intuitive and beatifying.
claims: Cognition of God in himself as present object would be intuitive and beatific.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1109.summary: Seventh argument: two cognitions of different species cannot have the same object in the same power, since the same cause always produces the same effect unless agent or matter varies (Metaphysics IX). The beatifying intuition and the supposed non-beatifying abstraction would be such, so one is impossible, and it is not intuition, hence the abstraction.
claims: The same object in the same power cannot ground two specifically different cognitions.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1127.summary: Eighth argument, from the object: our embodied intellect relates to what is most manifest in nature (God and separate substances) as the owl's eye to sunlight (Metaphysics II), so it cannot know the divine essence clearly.
claims: The embodied intellect cannot clearly know the most intelligible beings.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1145.summary: Ninth argument, from the mode or medium: abstraction requires either a representative (species) or none. No finite species can distinctly represent the infinite God (an equivocal, inferior effect cannot be adequate to its cause), which is why species are denied in heaven. Without a species the cognition would be immediate and hence intuitive. Confirmed by the light in which all cognition occurs: not nature's (disproportionate), not faith's, not glory's (belongs to the blessed), nor an intermediate light (denied by the proponents). The author notes in passing that one can answer with another light sufficient given the representative, or by granting the intermediate light, which he thinks possible.
claims: No finite species can distinctly represent the infinite divine essence.
Cognition of God without a representative would be intuitive.
Every cognition occurs in some light, and none seems apt for such abstraction.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1228.summary: Tenth argument, from the state of the wayfarer: cognition repugnant to faith cannot be had by a wayfarer, who would then have formally contradictory cognitions; evident abstraction and faith are evident and non-evident, clear and enigmatic, about the same object. Faith necessarily involves inevidence and enigmatic obscurity (1 Cor 13; Hebrews 11, 'argument of things not apparent').
claims: Evident and non-evident cognition of the same object cannot coexist in one intellect.
Faith necessarily involves inevidence and obscurity.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1263.summary: A further argument: if demonstrative abstraction coexisted with faith based on authority, the two habits together would incline the intellect more than one alone; but adding authority to demonstration adds nothing to its inclination, so faith and abstractive science do not coexist. Ends the opposing arguments.
claims: Coexisting habits toward the same object would jointly incline more strongly.
Authority adds no inclination to demonstration, so faith and science cannot coexist.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1288.summary: The author's first conclusion: evident abstractive cognition of God, as defined, is possible to a pure wayfarer by divine power while he remains a wayfarer. This holds for simple cognition of the divine essence and consequently for scientific cognition of all necessary divine truths. He announces proofs from the object (the divine essence), the subject (the embodied intellect), and the mode or medium.
claims: Evident abstractive cognition of the divine essence is possible to a wayfarer by divine power.
Consequently, scientific knowledge of necessary truths about God is possible to a wayfarer.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1312.summary: First proof from the object: when two cognitions can have the same object totally and under the same ratio, whatever can be the object of one can be the object of the other. Intuitive and abstractive cognition can share an object, and whatever is intuitively knowable is abstractively (mediately) knowable. God is intuitively knowable (in the beatific vision), so he is abstractively knowable, though not by the blessed as blessed, hence by a wayfarer.
claims: Whatever is intuitively knowable is abstractively knowable.
God is intuitively knowable, so he is abstractively knowable by a wayfarer.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1341.summary: Second proof from the object: the only grounds on the object's side for denying abstraction would be that God is necessarily present, that his essence does not abstract from his existence, or that he is infinite and disproportionate. None suffices. Angels and the soul are maximally present to themselves yet know themselves abstractively. Existence itself can be known abstractively. And if infinity barred abstraction it would bar intuition too.
claims: Self-presence does not preclude abstractive self-knowledge, as in angels and the soul.
Existence itself can be known abstractively.
God's infinity bars abstraction no more than intuition.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1383.summary: Third proof: if one of two items can be known abstractively where they are distinct, it can be where they are united, since unity or identity does not remove intelligibility. In creatures essence can be known abstractively apart from existence (with immediacy of object, though not of representative), so also in God, even though his essence is his existence.
claims: Real identity does not remove the abstract intelligibility of an aspect.
God's essence can be known abstractively even though it is identical with his existence.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1407.summary: Fourth proof: being knowable both intuitively and abstractively is a perfection, not an imperfection, in a created object (being apprehended by several acts of one power, causing or terminating them in itself or in a representative), so it cannot be denied to God.
claims: Being knowable in multiple ways is a perfection.
No perfection can be denied to God on the side of the object.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1427.summary: Confirmation: a creature as known object can cause imperfect abstractive cognition of God, so a fortiori the divine essence can cause, or at least terminate as immediate object, abstractive cognition of itself. Concludes that this is possible on the side of the object.
claims: If creatures can cause abstractive cognition of God, so can the divine essence itself.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1446.summary: Scotus's further argument (Quodlibet q.7): to whatever object it is not repugnant to be known by the most distinct cognition short of intuition, it is not repugnant to be known abstractively by a wayfarer. The divine essence, being scibile, can be known quidditatively or quasi-definitionally, since (per Metaphysics VII) the objection to definitions of singulars applies to contingent existing singulars. Quidditative cognition falls short of intuition, which concerns the existing singular as such.
claims: What can be known quidditatively short of intuition can be known abstractively by a wayfarer.
The divine essence, being scibile, is knowable quasi-definitionally.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1496.summary: Answers an objection to Scotus's argument (that knowledge of God is only intuitive or through effects, as philosophers had it): the bar on quidditative knowledge of singulars applies only to contingent, mutable singulars, not to a necessary singular, so God can be known quidditatively and scientifically. Then begins the proof from the subject (the 'sixth' argument): a power beatifiable only by its most perfect act can be perfected in via by a less perfect act of the whole genus. The wayfarer's intellect is beatifiable only by intuitive vision of God, so it can be perfected by the less perfect, specifically different abstractive cognition.
claims: Quidditative knowledge is barred only for contingent singulars, not for necessary being.
A power beatified only by its most perfect act can be perfected in via by lesser acts of the same genus.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1564.summary: Argument a minori: it seems less possible for the wayfarer's imperfect intellect to grasp an imperfect created object imperfectly than to grasp God imperfectly, since imperfect objects seem more perfectly attainable; yet the former is possible, so the latter is too.
claims: If the less likely holds, so does the more likely.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1584.summary: Rebuts the claim that the intellect by nature knows abstractively only what it first knew intuitively (through sense). That order is not essential or absolutely necessary to the power, only to acquiring a species naturally. Prior intuition is not necessary in being, since phantasy and abstraction persist without actual vision and intuition does not contain the abstract object. Even if it were naturally required, God could produce abstraction without it, as he could produce volition without prior intellection. And if necessary only in becoming, it is an extrinsic cause, which God can supply.
claims: The order of sense-intuition before abstraction is natural, not absolutely necessary.
Prior intuition is not required for the being of abstractive cognition.
God can produce abstractive cognition without prior intuition, as volition without prior intellection.
Extrinsic causes necessary only in becoming can be supplied by God.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1658.summary: Even if intuition were needed to acquire the species, the wayfarer, once he has the principle, could have abstraction after the intuition ceases, which would not take him out of the wayfarer state. Aquinas grants that God could infuse species of colour into one born blind and that God impresses species in angels to know things never intuited.
claims: Abstraction can persist after the intuition that grounded it has ceased.
God can infuse species directly, as Aquinas grants for the blind and for angels.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1687.summary: Confirmation: God can reveal evidently to an unbeliever that he will be damned for not believing in the Trinity, and the damned know evidently and certainly that they are justly damned (else they would lack remorse). This requires knowing evidently that God is triune, not by vision (they would be blessed) nor by faith (not evident). Likewise, angels could naturally know evidently that Christ's miracles were true and that God does not witness falsely, hence that Christ is God, though the evil angel may have been prevented.
claims: The damned know evidently that they are justly damned, which requires evident knowledge of the Trinity without vision or faith.
Angels could evidently infer Christ's divinity from his miracles and God's veracity.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1743.summary: Further: by divine power someone could evidently know another's beatific vision without being blessed, as one can naturally know angels. If the light of glory were required, God could give it without the vision. The vision is an express representative likeness of its object (a verbum), and it suffices for knowing the object that one know such a likeness, since like is known by like. So a pure wayfarer can know evidently and abstractively the objects of faith.
claims: One could know another's beatific vision without being beatified.
The light of glory could be given without the vision.
Knowing an express likeness of an object yields knowledge of the object.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1776.summary: Argues that faith and science can coexist in the wayfarer about the same object, which implies the possibility of evident abstraction. Faith no more necessarily involves inevidence than opinion involves hesitation, and Aristotle (Ethics) denies that opinion necessarily involves hesitation, against those who held one cannot act against science but can against opinion.
claims: Faith and science can coexist about the same object.
Inevidence is no more essential to faith than hesitation to opinion.
Opinion need not involve hesitation.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1807.summary: Explains opinion: the topical syllogism generates opinion, the adherence to a conclusion as far as such reasoning can produce it. Fear (formido) of the opposite is accidental, arising from the recipient's weak adherence, equally balanced reasons, or other causes, not from opinion itself. Some opinions are held as firmly and certainly as knowledge.
claims: Topical syllogism generates opinion.
Fear of the opposite is accidental to opinion.
Opinion can be as firm as scientific certainty.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1844.summary: Further reasons that opinion and fear are distinct and separable: Aristotle in Physics III offers probable and (in his view) demonstrative reasons that the infinite is not in nature; fear decreases as opinion increases; one who opines can think he knows. Fear without opinion arises when reasons are equally balanced; opinion without fear is also possible.
claims: Opinion and fear vary inversely and are separable.
Fear arises from equally balanced reasons, not from opinion itself.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1883.summary: The inevidence of faith is a negation or privation of evidence, or an imperfection, and negations and privations are neither of the essence of an illuminating habit nor its per se attributes; faith, a light of the intellect, cannot have obscurity as an essential property. If inevidence means only lesser perfection, faith and science can coexist like whiteness and sweetness in milk.
claims: Inevidence is a privation and so not essential to faith as a light.
Faith and science can coexist as differently perfect forms.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1912.summary: At least the act of one can coexist with the habit of the other, as acts of intemperance coexist with the habit of temperance, even acts of unbelief with the habit of faith. So faith and science are not formally repugnant, and inevidence is accidental and separable from faith. Further: their causes (authority and demonstrative middle) coexist, or a believer who learns by demonstration that God is one would lose the merit of faith, which is absurd. An object can be known more clearly in the Word and less in its own genus; an angel can know itself abstractively and intuitively. Faith and science are not contraries and no motion runs from one to the other.
claims: Faith and science are not formally repugnant; inevidence is a separable accident of faith.
Authority and demonstration can coexist, so a believer who learns a demonstration keeps the merit of faith.
An object can be known simultaneously in different ways.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e1972.summary: Tenth proof, from the mode or medium: the cognition could occur through a species representing the divine essence distinctly and immediately, as ratio cognoscendi rather than as first known object, infused by God. Whatever object can be perfectly expressed by a cognitive act can be distinctly represented by a species, though less perfectly. The divine essence is so expressed by the beatific vision, so it can be represented by a species. There is no disanalogy between act and species.
claims: God can infuse a species distinctly representing the divine essence.
Whatever can be expressed by an act can be represented by a species.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2014.summary: Further: intelligence and memory are equal in their objects (Augustine, De trinitate X). The divine essence falls under intelligence by vision in the blessed, so it can fall under memory through a representative species. Confirmed by Paul's rapture (2 Cor 12), in which he saw God as the blessed do (Augustine) and afterwards remembered, and by Moses (Numbers 12), who saw God 'not in riddles' and later remembered. They remembered the act and its object through some species.
claims: Whatever falls under intelligence can fall under memory.
Paul and Moses remembered their vision of God through a species.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2053.summary: Further: it is no imperfection for a created essence to be expressible by both act and representative species, so this is no imperfection or impossibility in God; if an imperfect object can have an imperfect expressive species, a perfect object can a fortiori. Ends by starting to report another proposed mode, continued next.
claims: Representability by a species is no imperfection and so holds for God a fortiori.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2075.summary: Reports another mode some propose: God could infuse such abstractive cognition without a mediating species. The author does not regard this as a distinct mode, since such cognition, even if caused by God without a species, is always naturally apt to occur through a species, and so sets it aside.
claims: Abstraction caused without a species is still aptitudinally mediated.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2093.summary: Reports an argument used by others: whatever the divine will can do with God's present essence as secondary cause it can do without it; God by his will causes cognition of himself in the blessed with his essence concurring; so he can without it, and that cognition, abstracting from presence, would be abstractive.
claims: God's will could cause cognition of himself without his essence concurring as cause.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2115.summary: Rejects that argument: it would prove intuition as well as abstraction, indeed only the intuition of the blessed; not every cognition abstracting from presence is abstractive; and the divine essence is not an effective cause of anything apart from the will, else it would cause necessarily, not freely. The paragraph ends by beginning the next conclusion ('I conclude that a pure man...').
claims: The argument from divine will proves too much.
Abstracting from presence does not make cognition abstractive.
The divine essence causes nothing except through the will, else creation would be necessary.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2136.summary: Second conclusion: a wayfarer with divine help can attain formally scientific, truly demonstrative knowledge of God and his perfections, and so the articles of faith concerning necessary truths could be known demonstratively and abstractively. Scotus's argument (Quodlibet 4, 7): an intellect able to have a concept virtually including all necessary truths about an object can have demonstrative science of it, and the wayfarer's intellect can, as shown. Such science would be theology in the truest sense, yet its possessor could not teach it, since its terms are not naturally knowable quidditatively, although Aristotle makes the ability to teach the sign of knowledge (Metaphysics I).
claims: A wayfarer can by divine aid have demonstrative science of necessary truths about God.
Articles of faith about necessary truths could then be demonstratively known.
Such theological science could not be taught, since its terms are not naturally graspable.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2193.summary: Second article, on intuitive cognition. Reports an opinion that a wayfarer can by divine power have intuitive vision of God while remaining a wayfarer. First argument: perpetuity of the beatific act belongs to beatitude, but a wayfarer can have the vision fleetingly, as Paul did, without being blessed.
claims: Perpetuity is essential to beatitude.
A transitory vision of God, as Paul's, does not beatify.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2211.summary: Second argument: one cannot be blessed without enjoying God (Augustine, De doctrina christiana I), but God can give intuitive vision without enjoyment by love, since he can produce any essentially prior absolute form without the posterior; so a non-blessed person, a wayfarer, could see God.
claims: Beatitude requires fruition.
God can give vision without fruition, so vision does not make one blessed.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2231.summary: Third argument: immortality of the flesh belongs to human beatitude (Christ was a wayfarer by mortality of flesh); yet with mortal flesh one can have divine vision, as Paul did and as Jerome says of some at the point of death.
claims: Immortality of the flesh belongs to beatitude.
Mortal persons have had the vision of God.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2249.summary: Rejects the opinion: the divine vision is essentially formal beatitude of the intellect, and such a form cannot be in a subject, permanently or transitorily, without making it blessed, as whiteness makes white, and so placing it out of the wayfarer state. Perpetuity is not of the essence of beatitude: beatitude lasting one day is as much beatitude as one lasting forever, though perpetuity is annexed by the ordination of divine goodness.
claims: The vision of God is formally beatitude and necessarily makes its subject blessed.
Perpetuity is not essential to beatitude but annexed to it by divine ordination.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2291.summary: Further: nothing can both have and not have its end; a pure wayfarer lacks his end, and the vision is that end, so it is contradictory for him to have it.
claims: A wayfarer having the vision is a contradiction, since the vision is the end he lacks.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2303.summary: Further: hope, proper to the wayfarer, and vision do not coexist, since hope is of what is not possessed (Romans 8, 'hope that is seen is not hope'); otherwise hope would not differ from joy.
claims: Hope and vision are incompatible.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2316.summary: Further: on the opponents' own view vision is more principally beatitude than fruition; if vision could exist without beatitude, so could fruition, and so both.
claims: If vision does not beatify, neither does fruition.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2325.summary: Concludes that a pure wayfarer cannot have intuitive cognition of God, citing Exodus 33 ('no man shall see me and live', that is, the life of a pure wayfarer). Ends the second article and introduces the third.
claims: Intuitive vision of God is impossible to a pure wayfarer.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2345.summary: Third article: replies first to the arguments against abstractive cognition. To the first: the minor (that abstraction always derives from intuition) holds only for acquiring abstraction from sensibles through sense, memory, and experience. God has no abstractive cognition at all, knowing everything other than himself intuitively, so the example fails.
claims: Abstraction depends on intuition only in the natural acquisition of knowledge from sense.
God has no abstractive cognition.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2371.summary: On the angel: an angel knows God naturally and so abstractively, not intuitively, so abstraction of God does not presuppose intuition of God. Prior intuition is needed only to acquire a representative principle or to know one thing through another; God can infuse a representative of himself without vision, and even if vision preceded, abstraction could remain after it ceased. The objection would also rule out faith and our theology, which are abstractive. Rejects a fallback that only evident abstraction requires prior intuition.
claims: Angels know God naturally by abstraction without prior intuition of him.
Prior intuition is only needed to acquire a representative principle, which God can infuse.
The objection would wrongly exclude faith and theology.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2432.summary: Reply to the second argument: the major is false. What is known abstractively can be supreme and perfect being, not known as potential or imperfect in itself, though known imperfectly. Abstraction 'abstracts from existence' only in that the object's existence is accidental relative to the cognition, which is compatible with its being necessary in itself.
claims: Abstractive cognition does not represent its object as potential or imperfect.
The accidentality of existence is relative to the cognition, not absolute.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2457.summary: Reply to the third argument: the minor is false taken universally; actual being, however present, does not always cause intuition, but only when known with the twofold immediacy described.
claims: Presence of an actual object does not suffice for intuition without immediacy.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2468.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: the consequence fails. Abstractive cognition of a real object relates to it even if first known abstractively. Cognition can be of the non-existent in itself, or by absolute power in a representative; science then does not relate really to its object, as often happens when the object no longer exists. If Aristotle meant otherwise, the author denies it, since there is no real relation to non-being. The arguments can be turned against their proponents.
claims: Knowledge need not bear a real relation to its object, since there is no real relation to non-being.
Science persists when its object no longer exists.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2505.summary: Reply to the fifth argument: the abstraction would be less perfect than intuition, and God's knowledge of creatures is and always was intuitive, not abstractive.
claims: Abstractive cognition of God is less perfect than intuition.
God's knowledge of creatures is intuitive.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2518.summary: Reply to the sixth argument: what is known in itself and is present is not thereby known intuitively unless wholly immediately; God can be known abstractively, mediately, as he in fact is by us.
claims: Being known in itself and present does not entail intuition without immediacy.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2536.summary: Reply to the seventh argument: one power can have two specifically different cognitions of the same object if something concurs in causing one and not the other (different media, or one immediate and one mediate), as physicist and mathematician demonstrate the earth's roundness by different middles and faith and vision bear on the same object. 'The same always does the same' holds of unimpeded natural agents, not free or equivocal ones. Different effects can come from the same agent and matter when the agent is equivocal. Even the same agent, God, could cause both.
claims: The same power can have specifically different cognitions of the same object through different media.
'The same cause produces the same effect' holds only for unimpeded natural agents.
An equivocal agent can produce diverse effects from the same matter.
concepts: faith and vision of the same object

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2599.summary: Reply to the eighth argument: Aristotle's owl text, if it denotes impossibility, refers to the power naturally and by common law, not to the object, which is most intelligible. The author does not claim such abstraction is natural, only by special divine help. Aristotle likely meant only difficulty, which he uses to show the difficulty of metaphysics, whose principal subjects are God and separate substances; otherwise his labor would be in vain.
claims: The intellect's weakness regarding the most intelligible is natural, not absolute.
Aristotle's owl image signifies difficulty, not impossibility.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2635.summary: Reply to the ninth argument: the cognition can be had through a species that, though finite, is proportioned to God enough to represent him, as the finite intuitive act is proportioned to express him and as the finite soul is God's image. No species or act represents God perfectly, but sufficiently. Denies that infinite intentional being cannot be founded on finite real being. Alternatively, 'being represented' is an extrinsic denomination of the object, God's being with a relation of reason that is objectively in the intellect only. Or the represented being can be called finite. Such cognition can even be actually immediate, though always aptitudinally mediate, which distinguishes it from intuition.
claims: A finite species can be proportioned enough to represent God.
Infinite intentional being can be founded on finite real being.
'Being represented' is an extrinsic denomination involving a relation of reason.
Abstraction may be actually immediate but is always aptitudinally mediate.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2716.summary: The confirmations (from the species' inferior order, its being an equivocal effect, and inadequacy) fail likewise: representation requires a proportioned relation, not equality, and an equivocal effect can be a ratio cognoscendi of another, as the species of whiteness is of whiteness.
claims: Representation requires proportion, not adequation.
An equivocal effect can serve as the means of knowing its cause.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2732.summary: Reply to the tenth argument: abstractive science and faith are not formally repugnant about the same object. The argument would equally exclude opinion with faith, which most grant. The inference 'not evident by faith, therefore inevident' commits the fallacy of the consequent (as 'not white wood' does not imply 'wood not white') and secundum quid ad simpliciter. Faith gives some evidence, being a light, though not scientific evidence. Even if it gave none, it would not follow that it causes inevidence, as prudence does not make one unjust. When inevidence coexists with faith it comes from elsewhere, like night's darkness, which is not caused by the stars that give it modest light.
claims: Faith and abstractive science are not formally repugnant.
'Not evident by faith' does not imply 'inevident'.
Faith gives a certain evidence as a light, though not scientific evidence.
Inevidence accompanying faith is not caused by faith.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2860.summary: Concludes that inevidence is neither faith, nor its property, nor caused by it; otherwise greater faith would mean greater ignorance and God infusing faith would darken rather than illuminate. Since faith is not essentially inevident, opinion not essentially fearful, faith, science, opinion, and even vision are absolutely compossible in habits and acts. It is no contradiction for an object to be evident through one habit and not through another, which is not 'in the same respect' (an ignoratio elenchi, like 'white by whiteness, not white by quantity'). Or: with science present, faith's inevidence is removed and faith gives only evidence from testimony, and the negation falls on 'by faith', not the whole composition.
claims: Inevidence is neither faith, nor its property, nor its effect.
Faith, science, opinion, and vision are absolutely compossible.
Being evident by one habit and not by another is no contradiction.
Faith yields evidence from testimony, not from the object.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2964.summary: Reply to the eleventh argument: faith does not make evidence from the object, but it does not follow that it makes inevidence; it makes neither, though it gives evidence from testimony or at least adherence. Hebrews' 'things not apparent' means its object is in most cases and by common law not apparent, not as an intrinsic condition. Or it means not apparent in relation to faith, since faith does not make the object evident.
claims: Faith neither causes nor removes evidence from the object.
The 'non-apparent' character of faith's object is not intrinsic to it.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e2999.summary: Reply to the twelfth argument: science and authority-based faith coexist about the same object, each with its own adherence. Together they increase adherence not intensively but extensively. Authority for the conclusion is distinct from demonstration's inclination and does not diminish it. While a demonstration stands, authority for the opposite cannot be received. Reports another solution (that adherence is intensified by both and diminished by opposite authority) but holds to the first.
claims: Faith and science can coexist, each with its own mode of adherence.
Combined adherence increases extensively, not intensively.
Authority for the opposite of a demonstrated conclusion cannot be received while the demonstration stands.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3087.summary: Reply to the first argument for wayfarer intuition: perpetuity is not of the essence of the beatific act but annexed by divine ordination. If God gives the vision fleetingly he could conserve it perpetually, as he conserves Enoch and Elijah, so on that view a wayfarer could be blessed. Paul during his rapture was truly blessed in intellect and so not a wayfarer in intellect.
claims: Perpetuity is not essential to the beatific act.
Paul in rapture was blessed in intellect and not a wayfarer in that respect.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3122.summary: Reply to the second: one can be blessed in intellect and not in will, seeing God beatifically without enjoyment, though not perfectly and totally blessed. Vision is essentially the beatitude of the intellect and does not await fruition, which belongs to the will.
claims: One can be blessed in intellect without being blessed in will.
Vision is essentially the intellect's beatitude; fruition belongs to the will.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3142.summary: Reply to the third: beatitude of the soul is compatible with mortal flesh, as Christ was truly blessed in soul; those Jerome mentions were not pure wayfarers but comprehensors and blessed in soul.
claims: Beatitude of soul is compatible with mortal flesh.
Christ was blessed in soul while mortal.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3155.summary: Reply to the first principal argument: simple intuitive cognition would be neither a priori nor a posteriori as to its object, but from God and of God. Demonstrative cognition would be a priori, since attributes would be demonstrated through the essence, which is prior to them.
claims: Simple cognition of God is neither a priori nor a posteriori.
Demonstration about God would be a priori through the divine essence.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3171.summary: Reply to the second principal argument: the cognition could be abstractive even though God's essence does not abstract from his existence, since that is not required for abstraction.
claims: Abstractive cognition does not require that essence abstract from existence.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3180.summary: Reply to the third principal argument: there are two kinds of mean. A mean by participation in both extremes (pale between white and black) does not coexist with them. A mean by negation, or by order of disparate forms ranked by perfection, can coexist with the extremes, and the abstraction between faith and vision is of this second kind, so it is not repugnant to faith. The paragraph then begins the second preface or prologue to Book 1, a principium on the theme 'Principium loquendi Domino in Osee' (Hosea 1). Following Ambrose and Aristotle (Physics I), principles must be known first, and since God is the first principle of all things Book 1 rightly treats of him first.
claims: The abstraction between faith and vision is a mean by order of perfection, which coexists with the extremes.
A mean by participation cannot coexist with its extremes.
Book 1 treats God first because he is the first principle of all things.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3257.summary: Divides the theme verse to describe Book 1 under four heads: its primordial position, its act of speaking (scientific or sermonic), and its matter (with the fourth head given next).

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3275.summary: Fourth head of the division: the book's fruit.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3282.summary: Maps the four heads onto the theme verse: 'principium' (primacy of rank), 'loquendi' (quality of the act of speaking), 'Domino' (the capacity of its bosom, since the Lord is its matter), and 'in Osee' (goodness of its fruit, since Hosea means 'hoping in him' or 'his salvation').

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3300.summary: First, Book 1 is a principium by position, having priority among the four books like the first column, chariot, wheel, or trumpet. Applying Genesis 49 ('Reuben my firstborn... beginning of my sorrow'), it is a principle of subtlety for investigating and of belief for declaring, since 'Reuben' means 'seeing the son': the book teaches seeing the Son in the Father's bosom and narrates 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1).
claims: Book 1 holds first place among the books of the Sentences.
It teaches about the Son in the bosom of the Father.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3348.summary: Second, Book 1 is a principle of nobility as firstborn: the Master's firstborn, laid (like Christ in Luke 2) in the manger of students because there was no room in the inn, set openly where it can be found, and the beginning of God's ways among the other books, as Lucifer was noblest by nature (Job).
claims: Book 1 is the noblest of the Master's books, as firstborn.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3385.summary: Third, Book 1 is a principle of solidity for strengthening: a firm foundation like rock, the strength and refuge of the faithful (Psalm) in the truth of faith about divine things, applying Job 30 and Psalm 137 ('if I do not set Jerusalem at the beginning').
claims: Book 1 strengthens the faithful in the truth of faith about God.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3412.summary: Fourth, Book 1 is a principle of difficulty for labouring (for author, reader, and hearer), 'the beginning of my sorrow': the Master's toil in composing, expressed through Lamentations 1 and 2 ('arise in the night... pour out your heart'). Ends the first principal part.
claims: Composing and studying Book 1 involves great labour.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3456.summary: Second principal part: the book is commended as instructive in its act of speaking, expressing many concepts and truths about God: easy to grasp, sweet to soothe (the scroll sweet as honey, Ezekiel 3), sublime to receive (only Christ can open its seals), and useful for choosing (the book of life in which the elect are written). The Master can say of it John 6, 'The words I speak to you are spirit and life'.
claims: Book 1 instructs easily, sweetly, sublimely, and usefully about God.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3493.summary: Elaborates the fourfold instruction on John 6: it teaches easily ('words', instructing Catholics plainly), sweetly ('to you', soothing the truthful), subtly ('spirit', eluding and excluding heretics through spiritual teaching about the highest spirit), and vitally ('life', confounding sophists). Ends the second part. Then the third part: the book's capacious bosom, whose matter or subject is the Lord, described as place, city, temple, and heaven of the Lord, the Lord of most simple essence, noblest persons, most perfect form, and most powerful crown.
claims: Book 1 instructs Catholics, delights the truthful, excludes heretics, and confounds sophists.
The subject of Book 1 is God.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3589.summary: First aspect of the Lord as subject: simplicity of essence. 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one' (Deuteronomy 6): indivisible, non-composite, immutable.
claims: God is one, indivisible, non-composite, immutable.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3598.summary: Second aspect: nobility of the persons. Isaiah 66 ('shall I who give generation to others be barren?'): the divine persons have fecundity in generating, nativity in emanating, and liberality in spirating, with the Holy Spirit proceeding like a flame.
claims: The divine persons are fecund in generation and spiration.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3611.summary: Third aspect: perfection of form (Esther 15, 'very wonderful are you, Lord'): supreme knowledge (unsearchable), decency (unwearying), clemency (inexhaustible), and justice (unbending).
claims: God's knowledge, clemency, and justice are supreme.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3625.summary: Fourth aspect: power of the crown (Sirach 1, 'one most high creator... sitting on the throne'): power to exalt and to judge and command. Sums up that Book 1 treats natural unity, personal Trinity, perfective beauty, and imperial majesty. Ends the third part.
claims: Book 1 treats God's unity, Trinity, attributes, and sovereignty.

qrdBas-ae1109-d1e3651.summary: Fourth principal part: the book's fruit, 'in Osee' (hoping in him, his salvation). The end of the book is to hope in God and be saved in him (Psalm 62; Hosea 13, 'there is no saviour besides me'). God heals from mortal sin, carnal reproach, present exile, and final punishment, through infusion of grace, purgation of sin, return to the homeland, and bestowal of glory. Book 1 is Mount Zion, a mount of watching where the Lord is seen from afar, to be seen finally on the great mountain (Psalm 14). Closes with a doxology.
claims: The end of Book 1 is hope in God and salvation in him.
God saves through grace, purgation, homecoming, and glory.
Theology now sees God from afar; final vision comes in glory.

qrdBas-ae1109.summary: Prologue q1 asks whether a pure wayfarer can possibly have evident cognition of God beyond what natural sciences can attain. After defining 'wayfarer' (one tending toward but not yet possessing beatitude), 'evident' (assent caused by the object, not commanded by the will), the intuitive and abstractive kinds of cognition, and natural versus supernatural possibility, Bassolis develops a distinctive account of cognition. Intuition needs only that its primary object exist and be present, so God's eternal knowledge of non-existent creatures is intuitive, and God can cause intuition of a non-existent created object. The decisive mark is immediacy: intuition is immediate, abstraction always (at least aptitudinally) mediated by a representative. Against an opinion that abstractive cognition of God is impossible for a wayfarer, he argues from the object, the subject, and the medium that it is possible by divine power: whatever is intuitively knowable is abstractively knowable, sense-intuition precedes abstraction only by natural order, and God can infuse a finite species proportioned to represent him. So too is demonstrative, a priori theological science of necessary divine truths, though such science could not be taught. Intuitive vision, by contrast, is impossible for a pure wayfarer, since it is formal beatitude and perpetuity is not essential to beatitude. A long argument shows that faith and science (and opinion and vision) are compossible: inevidence is a separable privation, not the essence or effect of faith, which is a light giving evidence from testimony. The item ends with a second preface, a principium sermon on Hosea 1 ('Principium loquendi Domino in Osee'), commending Book 1 for its primacy, instructive speech, divine subject, and fruit of hope and salvation.
claims: Intuitive cognition is distinguished from abstractive chiefly by immediacy; God's knowledge of creatures, even non-existent ones, is intuitive.
God can cause intuitive cognition of a non-existent created object and can infuse species directly.
Evident abstractive cognition of the divine essence, and so demonstrative theological science, is possible for a wayfarer by divine power.
Intuitive vision of God is impossible for a pure wayfarer because it is formal beatitude.
Faith and science are compossible about the same object; inevidence is accidental to faith.
Book 1 of the Sentences treats God as first principle and leads to hope and salvation.
